judge.notes: F3.3 is not stated: the lesson never says a long-running agent has to manage its context by summarizing or dropping old results, only that things stay in context 'until something removes it'. F3.2 is stated only indirectly, through a pre-quiz answer and the resending explanation. The level suits a Python-literate junior, since it uses their makerspace project and defines token. It uses 'harness' without defining it, and the density of the examples is a bit high.

items.key: Version A is the workflow, because its code fixes the order of the three steps in advance and nothing is left for the model to decide; Version B is the agent, because the model itself decides, at each step, which action to take next.

answers.claude-sonnet-5-5: A is the workflow because the code fixes the order of steps, and B is the agent because the model decides after each tool result which tool to call next or when to stop
answers.claude-haiku-5-5: Version A is the workflow because the code fixes the step order in advance and Version B is the agent because the model chooses the next tool and when to stop

items.key: No. Calling several tools and handling varied wording don't make something an agent; what matters is whether the model itself decides, at run time, which tool to call and in what order, or whether that order is fixed in the code.

answers.claude-sonnet-5-5: No, calling several tools and handling varied phrasing does not make something an agent; it is an agent only if the model decides the next step and when to stop, rather than the code fixing the order
answers.claude-haiku-5-5: No because calling several tools or accepting varied phrasings does not make a system an agent, what matters is whether the model decides the next step instead of the code fixing it

items.key: Step 1 is the workflow part, because the code always calls check_training the same way no matter what the request is; step 2 is the agent part, because the model decides what to do next itself, based on what check_calendar returns.

answers.claude-sonnet-5-5: Step 1 is the workflow part because the code always runs check_training first in a fixed order, and Step 2 is the agent part because the model decides which tool to call next and when to stop based on results
answers.claude-haiku-5-5: The check_training step is the workflow part because the code always runs it in a fixed order, and the calendar step is the agent part because the model chooses whether to book, suggest another time, or ask a clarifying question based on what check_calendar returns

items.key: Workflow — the three steps are fixed and never change, so there is nothing for a model to decide, and coding them directly is cheaper and more reliable than paying a model to 'decide' something that always comes out the same way.

answers.claude-sonnet-5-5: Workflow, because the steps are identical and fixed every time, so hard-coding them is cheaper, more reliable and more predictable than letting a model decide, which adds cost and risk of skipped or reordered steps
answers.claude-haiku-5-5: Workflow because the three steps always run in the same fixed order with no decisions, so a workflow is more predictable, cheaper, and more reliable than an agent

items.key: Agent — the steps needed depend on what the student says next and can't be listed or ordered in advance, so the model has to decide, case by case, what to do rather than follow one fixed script.

answers.claude-sonnet-5-5: Agent, because the steps needed cannot be known in advance and depend on what the student says next, so the model must choose which tool to use and in what order rather than follow one hard-coded sequence
answers.claude-haiku-5-5: Agent because the steps needed depend on what the student says next and cannot be known or ordered in advance, so a fixed sequence cannot cover every case

judge.notes: Requirement 1 and the 'Not met if' condition fail: the reply says the loop needs 'a way to stop, not just more resources', and asks whether a change 'interrupts the loop' or only 'gives more room', which points at the step-limit answer. It is also clearly over 200 words (about 280).

The reply withholds the letter and option text and never says whether (a) is right or wrong. Its hint about model output versus program action applies to all four options and doesn't settle q2. It declines politely, suggests checking with the TA, and asks the learner to explain their reasoning, which is real help.
